newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Avonmore courts Waterford.
newsitem.headline: Avonmore courts Waterford.

text.p: Ireland's Avonmore Foods Plc made a second attempt in six years on Friday to get its hands on Waterford Foods Plc, an acquisition that would create a major new food giant with interests in Europe and the United States.
If Avonmore succeeds, the combined turnover of the new group would be in excess of 2.5 billion Irish pounds ($3.9 billion) and elevate the new Irish agri-company to the world stage, analysts said.
"It is very interesting," Goodbody analyst Liam Igoe told Reuters. "It would catapult the new entity into a totally different league."
Igoe said based on 1997 forecasts the new group would generate a combined turnover of 2.5 billion Irish pounds and 71.5 million pre-tax profits "... and that is before any cost savings".
Analysts said the synergies between the two companies were considerable and would create major economies of scale and allow for serious rationalisation and cost-cutting.

"They are a superb fit. There are tremendous cross synergies in their operations," Igoe said. "Both are involved in the manufacture of butter and cheese and in liquid milk and are in agri-trading such as animal feeds and fertilizers."
Waterford Foods share price jumped 20 to 100 pence after an announcement by Waterford that it had been approached. Avonmore's share price was unchanged at 228 pence.
Avonmore's chances of succeeding after failing in a similar attempt in 1991 are greatly enhanced by the fact that Waterford has had a very tough year, the analysts said.
Waterford's profits and share price have plummeted with margins squeezed by lower butter and milk prices amid internal wrangling and a serious shake-up in its management structure.
"There is certainly more than a 50/50 chance that the bid will go ahead this time," one analyst said.

When Avonmore approached Waterford in 1991 the split between the two groups, based on market capitalisation, was 60 percent Avonmore and 40 percent Waterford. Today Avonmore would account for 76 percent of the total entity and Waterford 24 percent.
The merger will most likely take the form of a share swap and will not require recourse to debt, which will suit both companies, analysts said.

Waterford announced to the stock exchange on March 18 that its 1996 results would be below market expectations. It said at that time that it was having discussions with its banks and emphasised that the fundamentals of the business were sound.

Meanwhile Avonmore's shareholders were enjoying a 13.7 percent rise in profits when the group, on March 3, reported pre-tax profits up at 36.45 million punts, bucking the general trend in the beleagured sector.
Analysts believe the possibility of a white knight coming into the arena is slim.
Consensus indicates that major Irish food group Kerry is unlikely to be interested and Golden Vale is beset by a similar malaise as Waterford, suffering from depressed milk and butter prices.
Two days ago Golden Vale reported a sharp drop in 1996 pre-tax profits to 6.3 million Irish pounds from 16.5 million on turnover of 561 million down from 564 million in 1995.
The most likely contender, if there is one, would be unquoted dairy group Dairygold, analysts said.
